body:
You have $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and $d$ is embarrassingly large: a quarter-million vocabulary features from a hashed bag-of-words, a few million one-hot interactions, a corpus of residual-stream activations at $d = 4096$. Yet almost everything you want to do with them — nearest-neighbour retrieval, k-means, a linear classifier — depends only on pairwise distances or inner products between those points. The Johnson–Lindenstrauss (JL) lemma says you can almost always throw most of the dimensions away. For any $\varepsilon \in (0, 1)$, there is a map $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^k$ with $k = O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ such that for every pair $u, v$ in your point set,

$$(1-\varepsilon)\lVert u - v\rVert_2^2 \;\le\; \lVert f(u) - f(v)\rVert_2^2 \;\le\; (1+\varepsilon)\lVert u - v\rVert_2^2.$$

The target dimension depends on $n$ but not on $d$. That independence of $d$ is why feature hashing, random projection, LSH-based retrieval, and nearly every sketching layer in a scalable pipeline work at all.

## Why this matters

The lemma is a tool, but a specific tool: it tells you when sketching is safe. If a downstream estimator depends only on the Euclidean geometry of your points — a nearest-neighbour query, the Frobenius norm of a design matrix, the pairwise cosine of a corpus — then a $k$-dimensional sketch is a drop-in replacement for the full representation up to $\varepsilon$ error, at $k$ that depends only on $\log n$. The constants are kind: $\varepsilon = 0.1$ and $n = 10^9$ give $k$ in the low thousands, regardless of whether $d = 10^4$ or $10^8$. The lemma also tells you when sketching is not safe. If your estimator looks at a single coordinate ("did feature #137 fire?"), there is no $\varepsilon$-guarantee: a random map obliterates per-coordinate information by design.

## The core statement, and a one-page proof

Fix a point set $X \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ of size $n$. Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}$ be the matrix with i.i.d. entries $A_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1/k)$, and set $f(x) = A x$. The key lemma — the *distributional* JL — is that for any fixed vector $y \in \mathbb{R}^d$,

$$\mathbb{P}\!\left[\, \big\lvert \lVert A y\rVert_2^2 - \lVert y\rVert_2^2 \big\rvert > \varepsilon \lVert y\rVert_2^2 \,\right] \;\le\; 2\exp\!\big(-c\,\varepsilon^2 k\big)$$

for an absolute constant $c > 0$. Apply it to each of the $\binom{n}{2}$ difference vectors $y = u - v$. A union bound says the probability that *any* pair is distorted is at most $n^2 \exp(-c\varepsilon^2 k)$, which drops below $1/n$ for $k \ge C\,\varepsilon^{-2}\log n$. So a random Gaussian matrix works with high probability. There is no obstructive point configuration — the statement is uniform over $X$.

Why does the per-vector bound hold? By rotation invariance, assume $y = e_1$. Then $\lVert A y\rVert_2^2 = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k} Z_i^2$ with $Z_i$ i.i.d. standard normal: a scaled $\chi^2_k$ variable with mean $1$. A chi-squared concentration bound — Bernstein, Hanson–Wright, or a direct MGF calculation à la Dasgupta and Gupta — gives the two-sided tail. The whole proof fits on a page, and the mechanism is squared-Gaussian concentration, nothing deeper.

The target dimension is sharp. Larsen and Nelson showed that for some point sets any linear embedding needs $m = \Omega(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$; a follow-up extends the lower bound to arbitrary (non-linear) maps over a wide parameter range. The lemma is not loose.

## What the map is actually doing

A useful rewriting: $\langle A u, A v\rangle = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \langle a_i, u\rangle \langle a_i, v\rangle$, where $a_i$ are the rows of $A$. Each $\langle a_i, u\rangle \langle a_i, v\rangle$ is an unbiased estimator of $\langle u, v\rangle / k$ when $a_i$ has isotropic entries with mean zero and variance $1/k$. The sketch is a Monte Carlo estimator of the inner product, and the "number of samples" is $k$. From that vantage, JL is a Chernoff bound on an inner-product estimator, lifted to all pairs by a union bound.

That view also predicts what sketching *cannot* do. Nothing in the construction says $\lVert A u\rVert_2$ is close to $\lVert u\rVert_\infty$, or that coordinate identities survive. The guarantee is $\ell_2$-geometric and only $\ell_2$-geometric.

A second useful consequence is the variance of the inner-product estimator. For any fixed $u, v$ and $A$ with i.i.d. zero-mean entries of variance $1/k$, one checks that $\mathbb{E}\langle Au, Av\rangle = \langle u, v\rangle$ and $\mathrm{Var}\langle Au, Av\rangle = \big(\lVert u\rVert_2^2 \lVert v\rVert_2^2 + \langle u, v\rangle^2\big)/k$. The variance scales as $1/k$ and depends on $u, v$ only through their norms and inner product, not through $d$. That is the quantitative content of the $d$-independence promised in the opening: the estimator's error bar is a function of the output dimension and the vectors' $\ell_2$ sizes, nothing else.

## Discrete and sparse variants

Gaussian matrices preserve the guarantee but cost $O(dk)$ per point to apply. Several variants trade constants for structure. Achlioptas showed that entries drawn i.i.d. from $\{+1, -1\}$ with scaling $1/\sqrt{k}$, or sparsified to $\{+\sqrt{3/k}, 0, -\sqrt{3/k}\}$ with pattern $(1/6, 2/3, 1/6)$, give the same guarantee up to constants. "Database-friendly," his paper calls them: no floating-point multiplications in the sign case, and a free sparsity gain in the ternary case. The Ailon–Chazelle Fast JL Transform reaches $O(d \log d)$ per point by preconditioning with a randomized Hadamard matrix before a sparse projection; this is the construction behind modern LSH-based attention and matrix-sketching routines. Kane and Nelson later gave sparse JL matrices with only $O(\varepsilon)$ non-zeros per column at the optimal target dimension — practically, the sweet spot for extremely high-dimensional, extremely sparse inputs.

Feature hashing is the extreme case. The *hashing trick* of Weinberger et al. maps a $d$-dimensional sparse input to $k$ dimensions by

$$f(x)_i \;=\; \sum_{j : h(j) = i} \sigma(j)\, x_j,$$

where $h : [d] \to [k]$ and $\sigma : [d] \to \{-1, +1\}$ are random hash functions. This is a column-wise ultra-sparse projection: each input coordinate contributes to exactly one output coordinate with a random sign. The authors prove an unbiasedness bound on inner products and show that cross-task interference stays exponentially small — enough for linear models on hundreds of thousands of tasks to share one hashed feature space. The connection to JL is direct: with signed hashing the inner-product estimator has variance $O(\lVert u\rVert_2^2 \lVert v\rVert_2^2 / k)$, and plugging that into a Hoeffding-type bound gives the same functional guarantee at the cost of worse constants than a Gaussian matrix.

## A concrete anchor

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d, k, eps = 1000, 5000, 400, 0.1
X = rng.standard_normal((n, d))

A = rng.standard_normal((k, d)) / np.sqrt(k)   # Gaussian JL
Y = X @ A.T

iu, ju = np.triu_indices(n, 1)
orig = np.linalg.norm(X[iu] - X[ju], axis=1) ** 2
proj = np.linalg.norm(Y[iu] - Y[ju], axis=1) ** 2
ratio = proj / orig
print(ratio.mean(), ratio.std(),
      (np.abs(ratio - 1) > eps).mean())
```

With $k = 400$ the ratio has mean $\approx 1$, standard deviation $\approx 0.07$, and the fraction of pairs distorted by more than $\varepsilon = 0.1$ is a few percent. Doubling $k$ roughly halves the standard deviation, consistent with the $\varepsilon^{-2}$ scaling. Replacing the Gaussian $A$ by Achlioptas's $\{+1, -1\}/\sqrt{k}$ matrix gives nearly identical statistics; replacing it by feature hashing on the same budget widens the tail but keeps the mean honest. The dependence on $d$ in these numbers is cosmetic: push $d$ to $10^5$ and the only thing that changes is wall-clock, not statistical accuracy.

The failure mode worth seeing by hand is adversarial, not random. If instead of i.i.d. Gaussian inputs you craft $X$ to have one dominant direction that aligns with the row null space of $A$ for a specific draw, you can make the empirical distortion arbitrarily bad. That is why the lemma is a probabilistic statement about $A$, not a worst-case statement about $X$ given $A$: the guarantee holds for *your* fixed point set over a *random* draw of $A$, and if you expose $A$ to an adversary who then picks $X$, the game is lost.

## What to do with it

Three operational calls. First, when a $d \sim 10^5$-and-up pipeline threatens to become memory-bound, ask what the downstream estimator actually consumes. If it is a distance, an inner product, a Gram-matrix norm, or a nearest-neighbour query — anything $\ell_2$-geometric — a JL projection is the right first thing to try, and $k$ is set by $\varepsilon$ and $\log n$ rather than by $d$. Second, prefer a sparse or hashed matrix in the limit: for truly huge-$d$ sparse inputs (hashed n-grams, feature interactions, byte-pair tokens) Kane–Nelson sparse JL or the Weinberger hashing trick beats a Gaussian matrix on wall-clock by factors that matter at scale, and the extra variance is usually swamped by downstream estimator error. Third, treat the lemma as an *existence* result for the right downstream task, not a license. Any per-coordinate statistic, any $\ell_1$ or $\ell_\infty$ norm, any task that reads single feature identities, falls outside the guarantee; use JL for the geometry layer, not for the semantics layer.

## Limits and open questions

The lemma preserves distances, not angles — not directly. The cosine $\cos \angle(u, v)$ is preserved to $\varepsilon$ only when $\lVert u\rVert, \lVert v\rVert$ are not tiny; the error is amplified when either vector is close to zero, since dividing by a shrunken norm blows up the perturbation. The bound is an $\ell_2$ statement with no $\ell_1$ or $\ell_\infty$ analogue of the same form; nothing stops a JL sketch from scrambling a quantile or an outlier count. The $\log n$ dependence also hides a $1/\varepsilon^2$: halving the admissible distortion quadruples the budget, which is why JL is best used as a coarse screen followed by exact computation on the shortlist.

The lemma says nothing about *data-dependent* dimension reduction. PCA, Laplacian eigenmaps, UMAP, and SAEs all exploit structure the random map ignores, which is why their $k$ can be far smaller — at the cost of a bespoke map per dataset and dependencies that make statistical guarantees harder to write down. The right framing is that JL is the lowest common denominator: the $k$ you need when you refuse to look at your data. If you look, you can usually do much better; if you cannot look, the lemma is why your pipeline still runs.

## Further reading

- Johnson, W. B., Lindenstrauss, J. (1984). *Extensions of Lipschitz mappings into a Hilbert space.* Contemp. Math. 26: 189–206. The original existence theorem, in a paper on Lipschitz extension problems. The modern "random matrix" phrasing is a later paraphrase of the same construction.
- Dasgupta, S., Gupta, A. (2003). *An elementary proof of a theorem of Johnson and Lindenstrauss.* Random Structures & Algorithms 22(1): 60–65. <https://cseweb.ucsd.edu/~dasgupta/papers/jl.pdf>. The one-page proof via chi-squared concentration used in this post.
- Achlioptas, D. (2003). *Database-friendly random projections: Johnson-Lindenstrauss with binary coins.* J. Comput. Syst. Sci. 66(4): 671–687. <https://infolab.usc.edu/csci599/Fall2002/paper/DR3_jl.pdf>. The $\pm 1$ and ternary constructions that opened the door to practical JL in high-dimensional data systems.
- Ailon, N., Chazelle, B. (2009). *The Fast Johnson–Lindenstrauss Transform and approximate nearest neighbors.* SIAM J. Comput. 39(1): 302–322. <https://www.cs.princeton.edu/~chazelle/pubs/FJLT-sicomp09.pdf>. $O(d \log d)$ per point via a randomized Hadamard preconditioner — the machinery behind many "fast" sketching routines.
- Weinberger, K., Dasgupta, A., Attenberg, J., Langford, J., Smola, A. (2009). *Feature Hashing for Large Scale Multitask Learning.* ICML; arXiv:0902.2206. <https://arxiv.org/abs/0902.2206>. The signed hashing trick, the device behind Vowpal Wabbit and most ultra-sparse-feature pipelines.
- Kane, D. M., Nelson, J. (2014). *Sparser Johnson-Lindenstrauss transforms.* J. ACM 61(1): 4. arXiv:1012.1577. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1012.1577>. Sparse JL matrices with $O(\varepsilon)$ non-zeros per column at the optimal target dimension.
- Larsen, K. G., Nelson, J. (2017). *Optimality of the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma.* FOCS 2017; arXiv:1609.02094. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02094>. The target dimension $k = \Theta(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ is tight even against arbitrary (non-linear) maps over a wide parameter range.
